hud.title: Quantum Computer
hero.title: The *Quantum* Computer
hero.text: A machine that computes with the rules of atoms, built from microwave cables, gold-plated copper and one of the coldest places in the universe. Scroll to take the tour, from the lab down to a barrier a few atoms thick.
lab.title: The computer is the small part
lab.text: The white cylinder is a refrigerator. The processor inside is the size of a postage stamp. Everything else in the room exists to keep it cold and to talk to it: racks of microwave electronics, helium pumps and a compressor.
fridge.title: Six plates, each colder than the last
fridge.text: Take the shields off and the chandelier appears. A dilution refrigerator cools in stages, from room temperature at the top to about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero at the bottom. Outer space is 270 times warmer.
fridge.stat1.label: Heat noise at 293 K
fridge.stat2.label: Heat noise at 0.01 K
fridge.stat3.label: Aluminium below 1.2 K
fridge.dots: The dots are heat noise: crowded and restless at the top, almost gone at the bottom.
wiring.title: Every qubit has its own cables
wiring.text: Microwave pulses travel down coaxial lines to steer the qubits. At every plate, attenuators strip out the heat noise that rides along. The answers come back up so faint that they need an amplifier at 4 K before anything can read them. A few lines per qubit: this plumbing is a big part of why scaling is hard.
lights.title: Switch off the daylight
lights.text: …and you see what actually moves: microwave pulses going down, faint echoes coming back. From here on, everything that carries a signal glows.
chip.title: 97 qubits on a postage stamp
chip.text: Under the last shield sits the processor: a sliver of silicon with a pattern of aluminium on top. Each cross is one qubit. The lines around them carry pulses in and answers out.
qubit.title: An atom you can draw
qubit.text: A cross of aluminium, less than a millimetre across, cooled until it superconducts. Together with one tiny junction it behaves like a single atom with two energy levels. Call them 0 and 1. They sit about 5 GHz apart, which is why the controls are microwaves.
junction.title: A barrier a few atoms thick
junction.text: Two layers of aluminium, separated by one to two nanometres of oxide. Pairs of electrons tunnel straight through it. This Josephson junction is the one component that turns an ordinary circuit into a qubit.
state.title: Not 0, not 1, a point on a sphere
state.text: A bit is a switch. A qubit is an arrow that can point anywhere on a sphere. The poles are 0 and 1, and everywhere else is a blend of both. Looking forces it to choose.
state.hint: Press H, then Measure. Repeat a few times.
gates.title: Neighbours that share one state
gates.text: Qubits talk only to their nearest neighbours, through couplers. A two-qubit gate entangles them: afterwards neither has a state of its own, only the pair does. Each extra qubit doubles what the chip holds in play at once.
gates.stat1.label: One gate takes
gates.stat2.label: A qubit lasts
gates.stat3.label: 97 qubits span
qec.title: Many fragile qubits, one reliable one
qec.text: A qubit goes wrong about once in every few hundred operations. So one logical qubit is spread across many physical ones. Checks between them run nearly a million times a second, and a classical decoder undoes each error without ever looking at the data.
qec.stat1.label: Physical qubits
qec.stat2.label: Survives
qec.stat3.label: Logical error per cycle
qec.note: Error rates measured on Google's Willow chip, 2024.
qec.hint.mouse: Click qubits to flip them. Try several at once.
qec.hint.touch: Tap qubits to flip them. Try several at once.
qec.status.run: Cycle {cycles} · {caught} errors caught · logical qubit intact
qec.status.fail: {n} errors at once · too many for distance {d} · logical qubit lost
scale.title: One fridge is not enough
scale.text: A useful machine needs hundreds of logical qubits, each built from hundreds of physical ones. That means many refrigerators wired into one computer, with classical supercomputers beside them doing the decoding.
scale.stat1.label: Chips today
scale.stat2.label: IBM's plan for 2029
scale.stat3.label: To break RSA-2048
use.title: Not faster. Different.
use.text: A quantum computer will not replace the gigafactory next door. It is a specialist: simulating molecules and materials the way nature computes them, and factoring the large numbers that today's encryption relies on. Luxembourg is getting its own. MeluXina-Q is planned to start with at least ten semiconductor spin qubits, a different kind of qubit from the one in this tour, wired into the MeluXina supercomputer in Bissen.
